NEW DELHI: DMK on Wednesday supported the Tamil Nadu government’s resolution opposing the Centre’s proposed delimitation exercise, with Leader of Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin saying the state’s representation in the Lok Sabha should not be reduced.He said the number of Members of Parliament from Tamil Nadu should not be reduced in the name of delimitation and called for the exercise to be deferred for 25 years."In the name of constituency delimitation, the number of Members of Parliament should not be reduced. Our stand is that constituency delimitation should not be carried out for the next 25 years. We welcome the resolution on the 33% reservation for women. Our firm stand is that Tamil Nadu should not be affected by constituency delimitation. The movement that first told India what the impact of delimitation would be is the DMK," Udhayanidhi added.The development comes after Tamil Nadu assembly on Wednesday passed a resolution in the state Assembly opposing the Union government’s proposed delimitation exercise.Speaking in the assembly, CM Vijay also called for the implementation of 33 per cent reservation for women in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections based on the existing 543 constituencies."The 33% reservation for women should be implemented in the 2029 Lok Sabha elections itself, based on the existing 543 constituencies. The 33% reservation for women should not be delayed any further. In Tamil Nadu, more women have voted than men. Providing reservation for women is not a concession; it is a matter of social justice. The 33% reservation for women must be implemented without any further delay," he said.The resolution seeks to safeguard the political representation of southern states, particularly Tamil Nadu, arguing that their success in controlling population growth should not result in reduced representation in Parliament."All the states including Tamil Nadu and the people / elected representatives of the union territories have not had their population counted for more than 50 years. The next census to count the population was supposed to be held in 2026. Therefore, since the delimitation of constituencies has not been carried out for the last 50 years, based on the 2011 population census, the constituencies should be delimited and the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly members should be increased from 550 to 850 by bringing in a constitutional amendment Bill," the resolution stated.The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16, proposing to increase the strength of the Lower House to 850 seats and expedite the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill passed in 2023. However, the Bill failed to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and was not passed.While the Congress and other opposition parties have supported the Women's Reservation Bill, they have opposed the proposed delimitation exercise and called for an increase in the number of Lok Sabha seats. The Opposition has also demanded that women's reservation be delinked from delimitation.
Article Summary: DMK supports Tamil Nadu government's resolution opposing Centre's proposed delimitation exercise. Leader of Opposition Udhayanidhi Stalin says state's representation in Lok Sabha should not be reduced. Tamil Nadu assembly on Wednesday passed a resolution in the state Assembly opposing the Union government's proposed exercise.

Article Title: 5 indigenous small modular reactors targeted by 2033, Jitendra Singh tells LS
Article Text:
Union MoS Jitendra Singh speaks in the Lok Sabha during the Monsoon session of Parliament

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: A key objective of the govt under the Nuclear Energy Mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033, minister for department of atomic energy Jitendra Singh said in a written reply in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous SMR technologies, including the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200) and 55 MWe SMR-55 for power generation. BARC is also developing a high temperature gas cooled reactor (HTGCR) of up to 5 MW capacity, which can be coupled with a suitable thermochemical cycle for hydrogen production.Singh said India is steadily strengthening its indigenous nuclear energy ecosystem with a focus on advanced reactor technologies, SMRs, domestic manufacturing capabilities, private-sector participation and long-term utilisation of the country’s abundant thorium resources. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition. This includes deployment of large indigenous reactors such as 700 MWe pressurised heavy water reactors (PHWRs) and advanced reactor designs at greenfield sites, alongside development and deployment of SMRs at brownfield locations, including retiring fossil-fuel-based power plants, captive plants for energy-intensive industries and off-grid applications in remote areas.The minister also highlighted continuing work of the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) in advancing the second stage of India’s nuclear power programme. IGCAR is pursuing multidisciplinary scientific research and advanced engineering development for sodium cooled fast breeder reactors and associated closed fuel-cycle facilities, technologies that remain a cornerstone of India’s long-term nuclear strategy.On thorium, Singh said India is pursuing its three-stage nuclear power programme, based on a closed fuel cycle, to optimise utilisation of its uranium resources and progressively harness its abundant thorium reserves. Thorium, being a fertile material, needs to be converted into fissile uranium-233 in a nuclear reactor before it can be used for energy generation.India has already undertaken sustained R&D towards thorium utilisation. Thorium Oxide (Thoria) pellets have been used in the initial cores of operating PHWRs, while Thoria-based fuels have also been irradiated in BARC research reactors. The irradiated Thoria pins have been reprocessed to obtain uranium-233, which has subsequently been fabricated as fuel for the KAMINI reactor at IGCAR, Kalpakkam. Singh said the Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025 has been enacted to enable wider participation of both public and private entities in the nuclear sector.
Article Summary: The govt under the Nuclear Energy Mission is to develop and operationalise at least five indigenous small modular reactors by 2033. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) is undertaking the design and development of indigenous SMR technologies. The govt has adopted a two-pronged approach to accelerate nuclear capacity addition.

Article Title: Supreme Court pushes 19 states, union territories to notify cancer
Article Text:
Supreme Court has stepped up efforts to bring greater uniformity to cancer reporting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: With the National Cancer Registry Programme covering only a fraction of India’s population and rural cancer surveillance remaining particularly limited, the Supreme Court has stepped up efforts to bring greater uniformity to cancer reporting. The court on Tuesday asked the 19 States and Union Territories that have not yet notified cancer as a notifiable disease to consider doing so, a move that could make reporting of newly detected cases to public health authorities mandatory.Such notification could help plug gaps in cancer surveillance by giving health authorities a more complete picture of the country’s cancer burden, including where cases are rising and which populations are most affected. The data could in turn help shape policies on prevention, early detection, treatment capacity and allocation of healthcare resources.A bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant passed the order on a plea filed by a retired AIIMS doctor after his lawyer Gaurav Bansal told the court that NCRP covers only 10% of population and rural coverage is less than 1%.The push assumes greater significance against the backdrop of the WHO’s latest Global Status Report on Cancer, which estimates that 92% of people globally will be affected by cancer either directly or through a close family member.The report also projects annual cancer cases to rise to nearly 35 million by 2050.The Supreme Court was informed that 17 of India’s 36 States and UTs have already notified cancer, following recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare. The remaining 19 have now been asked to consider similar action.Dr Pragya Shukla, Head of Clinical Oncology at Delhi State Cancer Institute, said standardised, disease-specific and timely data was essential to track India's changing cancer burden, identify regional and demographic trends, and assess the impact of prevention and treatment programmes. Such a system, she said, would complement existing cancer registries, help identify high-burden areas, improve planning for treatment infrastructure and medicines, and strengthen evidence-based cancer control. Govil added that reliable data would be critical for planning prevention, early detection and resource allocation.The Indian Cancer Society welcomed the intervention, saying national notification could help build a comprehensive cancer surveillance system. “The Supreme Court’s intervention is a significant development, and we welcome its direction to the remaining States and Union Territories to move towards cancer notification,” said Jyotsna Govil, Chairperson, Indian Cancer Society, Delhi. However, she stressed that notification alone would not suffice and called for a uniform national framework with common definitions, reporting standards and data protocols to ensure comparable and interoperable data across states.
Article Summary: Supreme Court has stepped up efforts to bring greater uniformity to cancer reporting. The court on Tuesday asked the 19 States and Union Territories that have not yet notified cancer as a notifiable disease to consider doing so. The move could make reporting of newly detected cases to public health authorities mandatory.

Article Title: Rapido to process full medical costs for Bengaluru’s bedridden customer
Article Text:
Rapido will now cover Sani Krishna's complete medical bills after her accident





BENGALURU: When Sani Krishna,32, became bidridden mid-June following an accident which took place during her bike-taxi ride to work, she had one goal: To fight the aggregator until sufficient compensation is received and to demand accountability.Thursday, her two-month fight bore partial fruit as Rapido finally agreed to process the entire medical expenses through its insurance partner.A Rapido spokesperson told TOI that the process will be expedited.The mobility aggregator revealed that all bike-taxi rides booked through the platform are covered by an insurance policy for both customers and captains.This policy was, however, capped at a maximum of Rs 5 lakh in case of a claim, while her treatment had caused more than Rs 20 lakh.TOI reported on August 10 that while Rapido was willing to provide the maximum insurance claim under the policy, it did not accept to pay Sani’s entire medical bills.The accident occurred on June 17 while Sani was commuting between Byrasandra and Domlur for her work.A collision resulted in a tractor running over her.On August 6, Sani’s adv sent a legal notice to Rapido demanding an apology and compensation to cover the expenses fully.Rapido stated that it changed its stance as the accident was an exceptional circumstance.“Given the exceptional circumstances of this case, Rapido has also communicated its willingness to facilitate the processing of the entire eligible medical expense claim, without applying the standard policy cap, subject to the submission and verification of the requisite documentation by the insurer,” the spokesperson clarified.The aggregator also said it will ensure that Sani’s family receives the full amount towards her medical expenses under the insurance claim.While Sani had earlier claimed direct compensation from the aggregator instead of depending on a third party, Rapido explained that it is not permitted under applicable law to process insurance claims on behalf of an insurer.For Sani, who is currently recovering from what she describes as a near-death accident, the update marks a relief.She pointed out that the fight isn’t done, “Rapido still has not communicated to me their decision to insure the entire medical expense. I always had and still have belief that I will overcome this crisis. We also wanted them to take responsibility and apologise for the incident, and it hasn’t happened yet,” she expressed.Still unable to travel or work, the Bengaluru-based interior designer said she struggles every day.Sani underwent several surgeries, including plastic surgery for her face as she lost multiple teeth and fractured seven ribs.The circumstances of the accident, including questions relating to the captain’s authorisation and conduct are under investigation, Rapido said.
Article Summary: Rapido will now cover Sani Krishna's complete medical bills after her accident in June. The accident occurred on June 17 while Sani was commuting between Byrasandra and Domlur for her work. A collision resulted in a tractor running over her.

Article Title: Indian-origin man rejected for H-1B visa three times compiled 700 pages of evidence and spent $13,000 to secure another way to stay in US
Article Text:
A career in data and analytics

Attempts for H-1B

In June of the same year, he began preparing for the O-1 visa in June 2025, almost a year prior to the expiration of his OPT.

An O-1 visa

Since the onset of the second Trump administration, the H-1B visa has transformed from a government document into a coveted goal. From applying to the lottery numerous times to hoping for other visas and even planning to switch countries, people have done all things imaginable to be able to extend their stay in the United States.The entire effort is in response to Trump's tightening of visa guidelines to curb illegal migration while also prioritising native Americans. While the initiative has been impactful, it has led to displacing many people who were actively and effectively contributing to the United States economy. One such person is Sohan Sethi, a 29-year-old Indian-origin national who faced three H-1B lottery rejections before trying all his might to be able to get an O-1 visa.Sethi, was born and raised in Mumbai and spent 25 years of his life in India. Before moving to the US for his master's, he had never set foot outside the country. Since doing an undergrad overseas was not financially viable, he completed a bachelor's degree in computer engineering from the University of Mumbai and gained experience for about a year and a half as a business analyst while saving money and preparing for graduate school.It took him three years of continuous preparation, effort, and saving money to get to the US."While working full-time, I prepared for my GRE, gathered recommendation letters, and applied to several universities," he told Business Insider. The University of Illinois Chicago was his dream school and it had a business analytics program he really wanted to get into. Eventually, he got accepted and arrived in Chicago in January 2022."I had a wallpaper on my laptop of a bridge overlooking the Chicago skyline. Every time I felt exhausted or anxious, I would minimise everything on my computer and look at that picture. Twenty days later, on my 25th birthday, I stood in the exact same spot that had been my wallpaper," he said.As an international student, Sethi's fees were roughly $60,000 across three semesters. He received a research assistantship during his second and third semesters and the university covered a significant portion of the costs. After graduating in May 2023, he began working as a senior business analyst at a healthcare company. A year and a half later, he was promoted to manager of analytics and reporting and life was good.Sethi entered the H-1B lottery thrice and was rejected every time. "After my second rejection in April 2025, I realised I couldn't rely on the lottery alone if I wanted to continue my career in the United States," he said. In June of the same year, he began preparing for the O-1 visa in June 2025, almost a year prior to the expiration of his OPT.Unlike the H-1B, the O-1 isn't based on a lottery. Instead, applicants have to demonstrate "extraordinary ability" through achievements in their field. Thus, he hired a lawyer and spent the next several months building a profile while continuing to work full time. "I audited my achievements, secured media coverage, judged at industry events, received awards, published scholarly articles, and gathered letters of recommendation," he said.By February 2026, he and his lawyers had organised more than 700 pages of supporting evidence. For all of this, Sethi spent a whopping $13,000 on lawyer fees. In March, he was rejected from the H-1B lottery for the third time. "At that point, my STEM OPT was due to expire on July 5, leaving me with around 100 days to legally stay in the United States unless another pathway worked out," he shared.In April, he had filed for an O-1 petition. After filing, he received a Request for Evidence, which required him to submit additional documentation and wait again. Sethi said that while waiting for a response, he began thinking about other possibilities. "I know people who have gone back to their home countries, pursued a second master's degree, or moved to places like Canada or the United Kingdom. I considered those options too, but I couldn't find another country where I felt I could build the same career," he confessed.The O-1 visa is a temporary, non-immigrant visa for people with extraordinary ability or achievement in sciences, arts, education, business, athletics or television/film. It has no annual cap, no lottery, allows unlimited one-year extensions and requires a US employer or agent sponsor.As a professional working in data analytics and AI, he said no other country offered the opportunities, infrastructure and exposure that the US did. "That's why I didn't want to give up without exploring every possible option," he added. Eventually, his O-1 visa was approved and now, Sethi manages a team of analysts working in healthcare data and analytics.All this time, he had been sharing his experience on LinkedIn in order to guide others like him who felt uncertain and were navigating the O-1 process. "The only intent behind that was to be there for someone in the way I wish someone had been there for me. For now, my focus is on making the most of the next three years in the United States," he added.
Article Summary: Sohan Sethi, a 29-year-old Indian-origin national, faced three H-1B lottery rejections before trying all his might to be able to get an O-1 visa. It took him three years of continuous preparation, effort, and saving money to get to the US.

Article Title: An entrepreneur spent $1.4 million buying a 300-acre California ghost town, then moved in and began rebuilding it as a business
Article Text:
Representative Image of a restored historic mining town with 19th-century buildings and mountain scenery (AI-generated image)

How a $1.4 million bid won the race for California's ghost town

What Underwood found on 300 acres of remote, largely untouched 19th-century mining infrastructure

Why a fire in June 2020 destroyed the town's centrepiece hotel less than two years after Underwood bought the property

Why turning a ghost town into a working business has taken years of rebuilding, and counting

In July 2018, entrepreneur Brent Underwood, along with business partner Jon Bier, purchased the abandoned mining town of Cerro Gordo in California's Inyo Mountains for $1.4 million. The deal, which closed on Friday the 13th, included more than 300 acres of land and 22 surviving structures, among them a 19th-century hotel, a bunkhouse and a former superintendent's house. Cerro Gordo had first grown into a boomtown after silver was discovered there in 1865, at one point becoming one of California's largest producers of silver and lead, before falling prices and a fire pushed the town toward abandonment by the late 1870s. Underwood, who had previously run a hostel in Austin, Texas, saw an opportunity to turn the deserted property into a hospitality destination while preserving its history, a project that would go on to consume his life savings and, eventually, his full-time residence. Underwood's journey stands as a striking example of how ambitious historical restoration rarely unfolds according to plan, requiring years of unexpected setbacks, financial strain and stubborn persistence before a long-abandoned town can genuinely come back to life.Underwood and Bier were not the only ones interested in Cerro Gordo when it went up for sale. According to real estate agent Jake Rasmuson, who handled the listing, the property drew about a dozen offers after going on the market at an asking price of $ 925,000, with some competing bids reportedly higher than the $1.4 million Underwood and Bier ultimately paid. The sellers, a trust made up of brothers who had inherited the property after it stayed in family hands for decades, chose the pair's offer specifically because their plan prioritised preserving the town's history and keeping it accessible to the public, rather than simply developing the land for private use. Underwood has said the purchase used every penny of his personal savings, supplemented by a loan and a handful of small contributions from friends who wanted to be part of the project. The decision effectively placed the town's future in the hands of owners whose goal was not to erase its past, but to preserve the remnants of its mining history for future visitors.Cerro Gordo sits in a remote stretch of the Inyo Mountains, reachable only by a mix of paved and dirt roads roughly 25 miles from Lone Pine, the nearest town with a grocery store. At its peak in the 1870s, the town supported a population of around 4,000 residents drawn by its silver and lead mining operations, but by the time Underwood took ownership, only a single caretaker remained on site. The 22 surviving structures had been protected from looting and the elements for decades under the previous family's stewardship, leaving Underwood with a largely intact, if deteriorating, collection of 19th-century buildings to work with, including mine shafts extending hundreds of feet underground that once anchored the town's entire economy.Underwood's restoration plans suffered a severe setback less than two years into the project. In the early hours of June 15, 2020, a fire broke out at the American Hotel, a building that had first opened its doors on that same date back in 1871. The blaze destroyed the hotel completely, along with an adjoining icehouse and a nearby residence once known as the home of a notorious 19th-century killer. No injuries were reported, and investigators later pointed to the building's old electrical wiring, combined with decades-old newspapers stuffed into the walls as insulation, as the likely cause. Underwood has described the fire as one of the most devastating moments of his life, since the hotel had stood as both the literal and symbolic centre of his plans to revive the town.Rather than a quick renovation, Underwood's plan to convert Cerro Gordo into a hospitality and tourism destination has stretched across years, complicated significantly by the loss of the American Hotel. In the years following the fire, work shifted toward reconstructing the hotel essentially from the ground up rather than simply restoring an existing structure, a rebuild that was reportedly completed by 2025. Progress across the wider property has also been slowed by the site's remoteness, particularly the lack of a reliable water source, a challenge Underwood has addressed through temporary measures like trucked-in water and pumping operations drawing from deep within the old mine shafts. Since March 2020, Underwood has lived at Cerro Gordo full time, documenting the town's slow transformation, including the fire and its aftermath, for a large online audience, turning what began as a real estate purchase into an ongoing, very public restoration project still working toward its original goal of welcoming paying visitors to stay.

The property includes more than 300 acres of land and 22 surviving structures, among them a 19th-century hotel, a bunkhouse and a former superintendent's house. In June 2020, a fire broke out at the American Hotel, a building that had first opened its doors on that same date back in 1871. Who is Gautam Rangarajan ?

What will Gautam Rangarajan do at No. 10?

Burnham's government overhaul

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appointed Indian-origin strategist and former BBC executive Gautam Rangarajan as an Expert Adviser on Structure and Process in a newly created role at 10 Downing Street.Rangarajan, who brings decades of experience in strategy, organisational transformation and media, is set to take up the position this week.Rangarajan is a senior strategist and media executive with more than two decades of experience across media, creative industries and public service broadcasting.Before his new government role, he spent more than 30 years at the BBC, beginning his career as a radio music producer and eventually rising to become the broadcaster's Group Director for Strategy and Performance.His experience includes developing strategy in rapidly changing markets, leading large-scale transformation initiatives and handling complex policy and financial negotiations.The exact details of Rangarajan's responsibilities are yet to be outlined. However, the UK PM's office said his appointment draws on his experience in corporate strategy and transformation.His role comes as Burnham undertakes a broader restructuring of the machinery of government, including the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.Rangarajan is expected to play a role in the planned transformation at the heart of the British government.Away from strategy and public service, Rangarajan also has a creative side. He describes himself as a professional choral singer and music producer, alongside his work in corporate strategy and organisational transformation.The appointment comes as Burnham reshapes his government following his recent rise to the role of Labour Party leader and Prime Minister.His administration has announced structural changes, including the launch of No. 10 North in Manchester and the creation of the Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet.While the full scope of Rangarajan's new role remains unclear, his appointment places the former BBC executive at the centre of the UK government's planned transformation.
